title: IPO
directAnswer: You can do at most k projects; each needs capital[i] to start and pays profits[i] on completion, which adds to your capital. Greedily, on each of the k turns, unlock every project you can now afford (capital ≤ current w) into a max-heap keyed by profit, then take the single most profitable one. Sort projects by capital so unlocking is a forward sweep; a max-heap gives the best affordable profit in O(log n). Total O(n log n).

remember.pattern: Sort by capital + max-heap of affordable profits (greedy)
remember.formula:
sort projects by capital ascending
for _ in range(k):
    while next project's capital <= w: push its profit into max-heap
    if heap empty: break          # nothing affordable, stop
    w += heap.pop_max()            # take the richest affordable project
rules: Sort projects by **capital ascending** so 'what can I afford?' is a one-way moving pointer — never re-scan.
The heap is keyed by **profit, not capital** — among everything you can afford, you always want the biggest payout.
**Greedy is provably optimal here**: capital only ever grows, so a project affordable now stays affordable; grabbing the max profit each turn never closes a door.
Use a **persistent pointer** into the sorted array across all k turns — affordable projects stay in the heap until chosen.
**Break early** when the heap is empty: if nothing is affordable, no future turn helps either (w didn't change).
In Python, negate profits to fake a max-heap on `heapq` (a min-heap).
whenToUse: Pick at most k items where eligibility depends on a growing resource (capital, budget, energy)
Each pick relaxes the constraint for future picks (profit feeds back into capital)
You repeatedly need the 'best available' among a dynamically growing candidate set
Two competing keys: one gates eligibility (capital), one ranks desirability (profit)
antiSignals: You must do exactly all projects → no choice, just sum profits
Capital does not feed back (eligibility set is static) → plain sort + take top-k
Picking one project forbids others (mutual exclusion / dependency) → DP or graph, not greedy
Profits can be negative and you may skip freely → different greedy / DP
remember.takeaway: When a selection problem has a gate that loosens as you pick (capital grows with profit), sort by the gate and keep a heap on the value. The sweep unlocks candidates monotonically; the heap always hands you the best one. This 'two-key' split — sort one key, heap the other — recurs in scheduling, meeting rooms, and dijkstra-flavored greedies.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise a greedy with a moving-eligibility frontier and prove the exchange argument, instead of reaching for DP. Then whether you combine sorting (for the gate) with a heap (for the value) cleanly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Heaping on capital instead of profit, re-scanning all projects every turn (O(nk) or worse), or re-pushing already-unlocked projects on each turn instead of using a persistent pointer.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the exchange argument out loud: 'capital is monotonic non-decreasing, so any project I can afford now I can still afford later — taking the max-profit affordable one first never blocks a better choice.' Then note the two-key split.

problemStatement:
Suppose LeetCode will start its **IPO** soon. To attract investors, it wants to do some projects to maximize its capital before the IPO. Since it has limited resources, it can finish at most `k` distinct projects before the IPO.

You are given `n` projects where the `i`-th project has a pure profit `profits[i]` and a minimum capital `capital[i]` needed to start it.

Initially, you have `w` capital. When you finish a project, you obtain its pure profit and that profit is **added** to your total capital.

Pick a list of **at most** `k` distinct projects to maximize your final capital, and return *the final maximized capital*.
understanding: You start with capital w. A project is startable only if its required capital ≤ your current capital. Finishing it adds its profit to your capital (profits are non-negative, so capital never shrinks). You may finish at most k projects, each at most once. Maximize the final capital.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can profits be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — constraints say profits[i] ≥ 0. That's why greedy is safe: every project you complete only helps, so you always want to do as many of the best ones as you can afford.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must I do exactly k projects, or at most k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most k. If at some point nothing is affordable, you stop early — but since profits are non-negative you'd never *choose* to stop while something affordable remains.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can two projects have the same capital requirement?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Sorting by capital handles ties fine; both get unlocked at the same threshold and the heap ranks them by profit.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the answer just 'pick the k highest profits'?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — a high-profit project may be unaffordable until you've done cheaper ones to grow your capital. Affordability is the constraint that makes this interesting.

examples.explanation: Start with w=0; only project 0 (capital 0) is affordable → do it, profit 1, w=1. Now projects 1 and 2 (capital 1) are affordable; pick the bigger profit 3 → w=4. That's 2 projects; final capital 4.
w=0 → do project 0 (profit 1), w=1 → do project 1 (profit 2), w=3 → do project 2 (profit 3), w=6. All three affordable in sequence.
The only project needs capital 5 but you have 2. Nothing is affordable, the heap is empty on turn 1, so you stop. Final capital stays 2.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Rescan for Best Affordable Each Turn
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to anchor the greedy idea before optimizing the 'find best affordable' step with a heap.
hints: Capital only grows. So once you can afford a project you can always afford it. Does that suggest you should ever 'save' a cheap project for later?
On each of the k turns, what single project should you do? The most profitable one you can currently afford — doing it can only raise your capital and unlock more.
Implement that literally: each turn, scan all not-yet-done projects, pick the affordable one with max profit, mark it done, add its profit. Repeat k times.
approaches.complexityReasoning: k turns, each scanning up to n projects to find the best affordable one = O(k·n). With k, n up to 10⁵ that's 10¹⁰ — too slow, but it makes the greedy correct and obvious.
approaches.explanation:
The core realisation is that this is a **greedy** problem, not a DP one. Why? Because your capital is **monotonically non-decreasing** — every completed project has profit ≥ 0, so finishing it never reduces what you can afford next. That single fact powers an exchange argument: any project affordable on this turn remains affordable on every future turn, so there is never a reason to *skip* the most profitable affordable project in favour of a cheaper one. Taking the richest affordable project each turn is locally optimal *and* never blocks a globally better choice later.

**Why 'most profitable affordable' and not 'cheapest' or 'highest profit overall'.** Cheapest ignores payout — you'd waste turns on tiny profits. Highest-profit-overall ignores affordability — you might pick a project you literally cannot start. The sweet spot is the join of the two constraints: among the set you *can* start right now, take the one that pays the most. That maximally grows your capital this turn, which can only expand the affordable set next turn.

**The brute-force mechanics.** Keep a 'done' marker per project. Repeat k times: linearly scan all projects, and among those with `capital[i] ≤ w` and not yet done, track the index with the largest profit. If you found one, mark it done and add its profit to `w`; if none is affordable, stop early (no future turn can help because `w` is unchanged).

**Why we don't ship this.** The repeated full scan is the killer: `O(k·n)` with both up to 10⁵ is ~10¹⁰ operations. The fix is to notice we keep re-scanning the same projects to answer two questions — 'which are affordable?' and 'which affordable one is biggest?'. Sorting by capital answers the first with a one-way pointer; a max-heap answers the second in `O(log n)`. That's the optimal approach below.
approaches.insight: Greedy is justified because capital is monotonic non-decreasing: an affordable project never becomes unaffordable, so grabbing the max-profit affordable project each turn can never strand a better option. That exchange argument is the whole problem.

pitfalls: Forgetting the `done` marker — you'd redo the same project and overcount profit.
Not breaking when nothing is affordable — wastes turns and (harmlessly) loops, but signals you missed the monotonicity argument.
Picking the cheapest or globally-richest project instead of the richest *affordable* one.

approaches.name: Sort by Capital + Max-Heap of Affordable Profits (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'sort the gate, heap the value' — the two-key split.
hints: You keep re-scanning to answer two questions: which projects are affordable, and which affordable one has the max profit. Can you make each answer cheap?
Sort projects by capital ascending. Then 'newly affordable as w grows' is just advancing a pointer forward — you never look back.
Push the profits of all newly-affordable projects into a max-heap. Each turn, pop the top (best affordable profit) and add it to w. Do this up to k times, breaking if the heap empties.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n). Across all k turns the pointer advances at most n times total (each project pushed once), and each heap push/pop is O(log n) → O(n log n) for heap ops. Overall O(n log n). Heap holds up to n profits → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The brute force wasted time re-discovering the same facts. The optimal version pre-arranges the data so each fact is cheap to maintain.

**Sorting by capital turns affordability into a moving frontier.** After sorting projects ascending by required capital, the set of affordable projects for a given `w` is always a *prefix* of the sorted array. As `w` grows, that prefix only extends rightward. So we keep a single pointer `idx`: each turn we advance it past every project whose capital is now `≤ w`, pushing those projects' profits into a max-heap. Crucially, `idx` is **persistent across turns** — a project unlocked on turn 2 stays in the heap (unconsumed) and is still a candidate on turn 5. Each project is pushed at most once over the entire run, which is why the unlock work is `O(n)` total, not `O(n)` per turn.

**The max-heap answers 'best affordable profit' in O(log n).** Once affordable profits live in a max-heap, the richest affordable project is the heap's top. Pop it, add it to `w`, and we've completed one optimal turn. We do this up to `k` times. If the heap is ever empty when we want to pick, nothing is affordable and — because `w` did not change — nothing ever will be, so we **break**. That early break is what makes 'at most k' correct even when fewer than k projects are reachable.

**Why the heap is keyed on profit, not capital.** Capital's only role is the eligibility gate, and sorting already handles that. The decision *within* the affordable set is purely about payout, so profit is the heap key. Mixing these up — heaping on capital — is the classic bug: you'd repeatedly start the *cheapest* affordable project and leave fat profits on the table.

**In Python, simulate a max-heap by negating.** `heapq` is a min-heap, so push `-profit` and negate on pop. Java's `PriorityQueue` takes `Collections.reverseOrder()` for a max-heap directly. Both express the same idea: O(log n) access to the largest affordable profit.
approaches.insight: Two competing keys, two data structures: sort handles the *gate* (capital, a one-way frontier), the heap handles the *value* (profit, dynamically growing candidate set). Recognising that a problem has a monotone eligibility key and a separate ranking key is the trigger for this 'sort one, heap the other' template.

Turn 1 unlocks every project into the heap; subsequent turns just pop the next-largest profits — effectively pick the top-k profits.

pitfalls: Heaping on capital instead of profit — repeatedly starts the cheapest, not the richest, affordable project.
Resetting the pointer `idx` each turn (re-pushing duplicates) — blows up time and double-counts.
Forgetting the empty-heap break — in some languages this throws on poll/pop from an empty heap.
Sorting profits and capital independently — destroys the pairing between a project's cost and its payout.

commonMistakes: Using a max-heap keyed on capital instead of profit.
Re-scanning or re-pushing all projects every turn instead of advancing a persistent sorted pointer.
Reaching for DP — this is a clean greedy because capital is monotonic non-decreasing.
Not breaking when no project is affordable, leading to errors on an empty heap.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Heaping on capital instead of profit
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The gate is capital; the choice is profit. If the heap is ordered by capital you keep starting the cheapest affordable project and leave the biggest profits unrealised.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while idx < n and projects[idx][0] <= w:
    heapq.heappush(max_heap, -projects[idx][1])  # profit
    idx += 1
w += -heapq.heappop(max_heap)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Resetting the pointer every turn
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Re-scanning from 0 each turn re-pushes already-unlocked projects, double-counting them and turning the unlock cost into O(n) per turn.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Polling an empty heap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When nothing is affordable the heap is empty; polling it returns null (Java) or throws (Python). You must break first.
